description: Run exactly one queued slice through this repository's Boundroom supervisor, then stop and report the handoff and the stop reason. Use when asked to run the next slice, advance the queue by one, or start supervised work in a repository that has adopted Boundroom.

# Run the next slice

This skill drives the supervisor that `Tools/boundroom-sync.sh` copied into the repository you are working in. That copy, its queue and its gates decide what runs. This skill only starts it.

## Before you run anything

Run each check as its own command. Don't join them with `&&`, `;` or a pipe: a harness with a narrow command allowlist can refuse the combined form.

1. Work from the repository root. Run `test -f automation/supervisor/run_next.py`. If it fails, stop and say: "This repository has not adopted Boundroom."
2. Run `python3 automation/supervisor/run_next.py --help` and read its output for `--single-slice`. If it isn't listed, stop and say the synced copy is too old for this plugin and needs a sync to a newer Boundroom release.

## The one supported command

```bash
python3 automation/supervisor/run_next.py --single-slice
```

You may append these flags when the user asks for them: `--dry-run`, `--include-blocked`, `--queue <path>`, `--handoff-dir <path>`, `--board <dir> --kanban-overlay <file>` (also spelled `--kanban-board`), `--board-backend local` or `--board-backend hermes`, `--memory-config <file> --memory-project <name>`.

A Kanban board can be a local board, which needs no Hermes, or a Hermes board. The overlay's `backend` says which, and the supervisor refuses a `--board-backend` that disagrees. Report that refusal; don't change the flag to get past it.

Telemetry is off unless the user turns it on. Add a telemetry flag (`--telemetry`, `--telemetry-file-dir`, `--telemetry-endpoint`, `--telemetry-capture`, `--telemetry-runner`, `--telemetry-required` or `--no-telemetry`) only when the user asked for telemetry in this request, with exactly the values they gave. Never choose a destination for them, and never put a header or token on the command line: those come only from the user's own environment or `~/.config/boundroom/telemetry.json`.

Never add `--autonomous-limit`, in any form. With `--single-slice`, the supervisor refuses it with exit 64 and runs nothing. Don't work around that refusal; report it.

## After it returns

Report:

- the exit code;
- the slice it ran, from the JSON decision report on stdout;
- the decision and stop reason;
- the handoff file under `automation/handoffs/`.

Then stop. Do not run the command again, start the next slice, schedule a later run, or loop. Only the supervisor decides whether work continues, and with `--single-slice` it has already decided to stop. If the user wants another slice, they invoke this skill again.

## What this skill does not guarantee

These instructions guide you; they don't enforce anything. The enforcement is `run_next.py --single-slice` itself. A plain `run_next.py` without the flag can run several slices, up to the queue's `consecutive_autonomous_limit`, and a caller can raise that limit. Don't run it that way from this skill.

tasks.title: feat(release): attest the release archive (SPEC-009 RA-ENT-003)
tasks.body:
SPEC-009 RA-ENT-003: each release archive gets signed build provenance that anyone can check with `gh attestation verify`.

## What changes in `release.yml`

The new **attest** job runs between `build` and `release`:

1. Downloads the files `build` staged.
2. Checks the archive against its `.sha256`.
3. Signs SLSA build provenance for `boundroom-<tag>.tar.gz` with `actions/attest`, pinned to the v4.2.2 commit (`1e69f48`, released 2026-08-04).

**Why `actions/attest` instead of the `attest-build-provenance` that SPEC-009 named:** since v4, `attest-build-provenance` is only a wrapper around `actions/attest`, and its README says new setups should use `actions/attest` directly. The provenance is the same, with one fewer action in the chain.

**Least privilege:**
- `attest` is the only job with `id-token: write` and `attestations: write`, alongside `contents: read`.
- It checks nothing out and runs no repository code, so neither the gate nor the dev dependencies can reach its signing token.
- It doesn't need `artifact-metadata: write`, which only applies when pushing to an image registry.

`release` now waits for both `build` and `attest`, so nothing is published unattested. The release notes include the verify command.

## Docs

- **Upgrade guide:** a new "Verifying a release" section with `gh attestation verify --repo … --signer-workflow …`, the checksum check, and a note that releases up to v0.4.0 have no attestation.
- **Workflow guide's Releases section:**
  - describes the attest job;
  - fixes the archive name, which was shown as `Boundroom-…`;
  - fixes the verify example, which still used the pre-0.3.0 `repo-automation-…` name;
  - replaces the MAJOR/MINOR/PATCH bullets, which contradicted the compatibility policy merged in #243, with a pointer to that policy.
- **Control map:**
  - adds the attestation control;
  - narrows the "Artifact attestations, SBOM" gap to the SBOM, which still waits on your choice of generator (RA-ENT-004);
  - adds the attest job to the least-privilege row;
  - changes action pinning from "process" to "enforced by a required check".
- **SPEC-009** records the slice as delivered.

## Tests

`test_release_workflow.py` reads the workflows as text, because PyYAML is only an indirect dependency. It fails if:
- the attest job stops using a pinned `actions/attest`, attesting the archive, or checking the checksum first;
- any job other than `attest`, or the top-level permissions, can mint an OIDC token;
- the attest job checks out code or runs `uv`;
- `release` stops needing `attest`;
- any `uses:` in any workflow isn't pinned to a full commit SHA with a `# vN` comment. All 30 are pinned today.

## Not verifiable yet

The acceptance criterion, `gh attestation verify` succeeding on a release archive, can only be met by a real release, and a release needs a tag you create or approve. The first release after v0.4.0 is the live check. If the job fails there, nothing is published, because `release` needs it.

## Checks

- `make reusable-check` passes locally (943 passed, 5 skipped).
- `mkdocs build --strict` passes.
- No supervisor code changes, so there's no performance impact.

tasks.title: feat(release): keep a changelog and publish it as the release notes (SPEC-009 RA-ENT-006)
tasks.body:
SPEC-009 RA-ENT-006: a changelog, and release notes that come from it.

## `CHANGELOG.md`

- **A section for every release, v0.1.0 to v0.4.0**, written from the pull requests merged between each pair of tags. Each section groups changes under Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed and Fixed.
- **An Unreleased section** for everything since v0.4.0: the telemetry upgrade and the OTLP header fix (#240), the generic runner prompt (#241), the sync allowlist and the deprecations (#242), the compatibility policy (#243), the attestation (#244), and the removal of Discord and Slack support (#238).
- **How to keep it up:** a pull request that changes what a consumer sees adds a line under Unreleased. The release pull request renames that heading to `## <version> (<YYYY-MM-DD>)`.

## Release notes from the changelog

`Tools/changelog_section.py <tag>` prints the tag's section. It exits 1 if the section is missing or empty, if a version has two sections, or if a heading can't be read, and 64 for a malformed tag. A prerelease needs a section of its own.

In `release.yml`:
- **`semver`** (the first job) runs the tool, so a tag without a section stops before the gate spends a run.
- **`build`** writes the section to `notes/notes.md` and uploads it as a `release-notes` artifact. It's kept apart from `dist/`, because every file in `dist/` becomes a release asset and the attest job attests that artifact.
- **`release`** publishes the section with `--notes-file`, followed by the commit and the `gh attestation verify` command. This replaces the generic one-line notes.

## Docs

- **AGENTS.md:** the release rule now asks for `Tools/changelog_section.py <tag>` to pass, next to `Tools/check_plugin_version.py <tag>`, before a person creates the tag. That's the only change to AGENTS.md.
- **Workflow guide, upgrade guide and README:** link the changelog and explain where release notes come from. The workflow guide also lists the new refusal.
- **SPEC-009** records the slice as delivered.

## Tests

- **`test_changelog.py`** fails if:
  - the changelog has no section for the version every manifest declares (`pyproject.toml` and the three plugin manifests);
  - Unreleased isn't the first section;
  - releases or their dates are out of order;
  - a released section is empty.
  It also covers each refusal of the tool and its command-line exit codes.
- **`test_release_workflow.py`** additionally fails if:
  - `semver` stops checking for the section;
  - the notes stop coming from it;
  - the notes end up in `dist/` or in the attest job.

## For your review

I wrote the past sections from the commit history. Please check that they describe each release the way you'd want consumers to read it, especially v0.1.0, which has little history to draw on.

## Checks

- `make reusable-check` passes locally (963 passed, 5 skipped).

tasks.body:
SPEC-009 RA-ENT-008: a support matrix, and CI that runs it.

## CI

**`lint.yml`:**
- Adds Python 3.13 and 3.14 to the `make reusable-check` matrix. They go after 3.11 and 3.12, because the `main` ruleset requires `make reusable-check (3.11)` and `(3.12)` by name, and those names don't change.
- Adds a separate `make reusable-check (macOS)` job on `macos-latest` with Python 3.12. It's a job of its own rather than a matrix axis, because adding an `os` axis would rename the required checks.
- The new jobs aren't required. Making them required is a ruleset change, which is yours.

**`release.yml`:** the gate runs the same Python matrix plus a `gate-macos` job, and `build` waits for both. So a release is never tested on less than a pull request.

## The support matrix

It's in the README, under "Versions and compatibility":

| Component | Tested |
| --- | --- |
| Python | 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 on Linux; 3.11 and 3.12 required |
| Operating system | Linux, and macOS with Python 3.12. Windows isn't tested or supported. |
| Synced copy in a consumer | Python 3.11 or later with Pydantic 2, which the sync checks before writing |
| Claude Code runner | 2.1.311 on macOS, from the RA-BD-004 canary. Not run in CI. |
| Codex and Hermes runners | Fakes only. Live canaries are deferred to an approved machine. |

The compatibility policy gains a row: adding a Python version or an operating system is a patch-level change, and dropping one needs a minor release that was announced in an earlier release. The CHANGELOG's Unreleased section and SPEC-009 record the change.

**One addition beyond SPEC-009:** the spec named 3.13. I added 3.14 too, because it's the current stable Python and the gate passes on it.

## Evidence

- **Locally on macOS:** the full gate passes on Python 3.13.18 and 3.14.10 (963 passed, 5 skipped on each). This PR's own CI runs the new jobs on Linux and macOS.
- **`test_support_matrix.py`** fails if:
  - `lint.yml` and the release gate run different Pythons;
  - the README's Python list differs from them;
  - 3.11 and 3.12 stop being first;
  - `requires-python` stops matching the oldest tested version;
  - either workflow loses its macOS job;
  - the release build stops waiting for both gates.

## Checks

- `make reusable-check` passes locally (969 passed, 5 skipped).
- `mkdocs build --strict` passes.
- CI gains three jobs per pull request: about 2 to 3 minutes each, run in parallel. Hosted runners are free for this public repository.
- No supervisor code changes.

tasks.title: docs: add the operator docs and a checked exit-code reference (SPEC-009 RA-ENT-011)
tasks.body:
SPEC-009 RA-ENT-011: operator docs. These four pages are drawn from the specs, the harness guide and the code. The specs stay the source of truth, and each page says so.

## What's added

- **`docs/reference/architecture.md`:** the components, one slice from selection to verdict, who owns each piece of state, how a release reaches a consumer, and what is proposed but not built.
- **`docs/reference/security-model.md`:** the assets, who is trusted with what, the controls and where each is enforced, and a section on what Boundroom does not protect against. That section says plainly that Boundroom is not a sandbox: during a session, the runner's own permissions are the limit.
- **`docs/reference/exit-codes.md`:** every exit code for the 12 command-line entry points (the supervisor's commands, `run_agent.sh`, the sync tool and the two release checks), plus every failure reason, every decision with its queue status, and the prompt and runner-rules error codes.
- **`docs/reference/troubleshooting.md`:** each `stop:` and `boundroom-sync: error:` message, with its exit code, cause and fix. It also covers recovering a slice stuck `in_progress`, which the docs didn't cover before.

They're linked from the README (a new "Operating Boundroom" section), `docs/index.md`, the mkdocs nav and the compatibility policy's exit-code row. There's also a changelog line and a SPEC-009 progress note.

## Acceptance: every exit code is documented, checked by a test

`automation/tests/test_operator_docs.py` reads the code without running it:

- It discovers every Python entry point (`if __name__ == "__main__"`) in `automation/supervisor`, `automation/context` and `Tools`, adds `run_agent.sh` and the sync tool, and fails if one has no section in the reference.
- It extracts each command's exit codes. For Python it uses the AST: literal returns and exits, names assigned a code and then returned or exited with (`EX_CONFIG`, or evaluate_handoff's `code = 0 if ... else 1`), and the `exit_code=` default. For shell it matches `exit N` and `return N` anywhere on a line, after removing quoted strings, comments and heredoc bodies. It parses every Python heredoc a shell command runs: the sync tool's whole program, and `run_agent.sh`'s sandbox probe. It fails if a code isn't listed, and if a listed code can't be exited with. The one exception is `swarm_wiki.py`'s 0, which is the compiler's own exit code.
- It finds entry points with the AST, so `'__main__'` in either quote style counts.
- It checks that the failure reasons match run_next's `fail()` calls and `session_error()`, that the decisions and their queue statuses match `policy.py`'s `CompletionDecision` calls, and that the prompt and runner-rules errors match the error codes run_next raises with `ConfigError`. All three are exact matches, so a stale row also fails.
- Guards stop it passing on an empty glob or a broken extractor. One checks that `"exit 75"` inside a quoted sandbox command in `run_agent.sh` isn't counted.

Mutation check, run locally. Each of these fails the test:

- adding `return 99` to `settings_view.py`;
- adding `exit 42`, or `cmd || exit 70`, to `run_agent.sh`;
- renaming a `fail()` reason, or a decision;
- changing evaluate_handoff's `else 1` to `else 3`;
- changing the sandbox probe's `sys.exit(1 ...)` to `sys.exit(3 ...)`;
- adding a new `Tools/*.py` entry point that uses single quotes;
- dropping `settings_view.py`'s `return 64`, which leaves a stale row.

## Things the reference makes explicit

- **A slice that fails its checks exits 0.** `run_next.py` records `stop_failed`, `stop_blocked` or `stop_for_review` in the decision report and the queue, then exits 0. A non-zero exit means the supervisor refused to start, or couldn't judge the slice. This was true before, but no page said it.
- **The autonomous limit gives `stop_for_review`, not `stop`.**
- **The runner's exit code passes through `run_next.py`.** So `run_next.py` can exit 64, 66, 69, 73 or 78 from `run_agent.sh`, as well as its own 2, 64 and 78. For 64 and 78, a printed failure report says the slice was claimed and is now `failed`.
- **A Git failure while the supervisor measures a claimed slice exits 2 and leaves the slice `in_progress`, with no failure report.** `_cli_entry` catches the `ConfigError` without calling `fail()`. The docs describe this and how to recover. Changing the code to fail the slice instead is a separate supervisor change.
- **In a run of several slices, a refusal keeps the earlier slices' verdicts.**
- **evaluate_handoff's exit 1 is also an unhandled error**, with a traceback and no report.

## Review fixes (second commit)

A code review found places where the pages and the code disagreed, and gaps in the test. The second commit fixes them:

- the 64 and 78 ambiguity;
- slices left `in_progress` after a claim;
- multi-slice refusals;
- evaluate_handoff's exit 1;
- the architecture diagram, which built the context after the claim, but the code builds it before;
- the ceiling, which doesn't cap `custom`;
- the extraction gaps and the two-way check described above.

## Checks

- `make reusable-check` passes locally on Python 3.12 (983 passed, 5 skipped).
- `mkdocs build --strict` passes.
- No supervisor or sync code changes. No new file, network or subprocess work in the supervisor paths.
